records.text: World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 3 US rates: moving with the data Mark Cabana, CFA BofAS Themes: softer data reduces urgency for Fed tightening Recent US inflation and labor market data suggest less pressure on the Fed to hike. July employment data showed moderation in hiring and wage growth, while inflation data were consistent with a softer core inflation trajectory. As a result, the urgency for additional Fed tightening has diminished and markets have moved toward pricing a more patient policy path. Our US economists still expect three 25bps Fed hikes in 2H ’26 (Sept, Oct, Dec) but see risks skewing later. We see Fed “jump risk” around the Nov election; if the Fed is not hiking in Sept, we believe it is highly unlikely they start in October. Historically, the Fed has never started hiking at the meeting immediately preceding a Congressional election. While US data has softened, rates remain elevated with hike and upside commodity risks. Further data cooling will see rates come down; as a result, we flip our US duration and curve views. We now expect lower belly US rates alongside a steeper UST curve. records.text: year. We attribute this to the steel and aluminum Section 232 regime, which lacks a USMCA exemption and is now impacting the metal content of these finished goods. This reinforces a critical pattern whereby compliance no longer guarantees duty-free entry when sectoral instruments target specific inputs rather than origin. Crucially, because Section-232-type measures lie outside the USMCA architecture, even a benign, negotiated outcome regarding rules of origin would leave this channel of effective-tariff erosion intact. In tandem with these US-led shifts, the Mexican government has moved to strengthen its own regulatory and protectionist framework. The Mexican tariff decree of 29 December 2025 raised MFN duties on 1,463 lines (around 12% of the schedule by number of lines) at rates of 5–50%, with a 50% ceiling on automotive components. This measure specifically targets non-FTA origins – primarily China and other Asian suppliers – while exempting USMCA partners . Given its legislative origin, this decree is expected to be renewed beyond 2026. Complementing this, the Mexican administration’s recent Customs Law reform (effective 1 January 2026) has tightened importer liability and IMMEX controls, notably by asserting that customs agents have some responsibility for inaccurate importer data. This signals a broader domestic trend towards increased regulatoryoversight and heightened compliance rigor. Share of sector in total USMCA compliance Calculated duty Free status 2018 2024 20

This is where the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company (HKPMCC), which began trial operations in July 2026, comes in. HKPMCC is often described as Hong Kong's answer to London's bullion market infrastructure. Like the LBMA ecosystem, it relies on unallocated settlement, internationally recognised good-delivery bars, bullion-bank participation and a network of vaults. However, unlike the LBMA, HKPMCC is a government-backed initiative specifically designed to build an Asian trading, clearing, storage and reserve hub while strengthening links with mainland China and the Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE). HKPMCC is therefore not an immediate replacement for London. The LBMA retains deeper liquidity, a larger vaulting network and the world's leading OTC gold benchmark. records.text: Russian refinery runs fell to 21-year lows in July and currently stand at around 4.1mbd. For middle distillates, Russian production declined around 350kbd between March and July, according to Kpler. Given significant outages and damage to Russian refineries, we expect flows to be heavily subdued even after the lifting of the export ban, with recovery of flows likely to take months rather than weeks, leaving gasoil markets tight at least for the remainder of Q3. Unplanned outage risks despite lighter maintenance: We expect September’s maintenance season to be relatively light this year, given strong refining margins and supply shortages. However, this brings risks of unplanned outages through the following months and into next year, particularly given how strong refineries have been running globally. Further, we have seen little hurricane activity so far this year ; this is another tail risk that could lead to unplanned outages for refineries in the coming months. Potential for respite in Q4: We see gasoil cracks peaking by Q4 should flows from Jizan, Russia, and Hormuz resume and ramp up, combined with the end of the maintenance season. However, winter demand and the need to restock will limit downside to cracks. Trade idea: We initiate a long Oct26-Dec26 gasoil crack trade as a result, as we think the sell-off at the front of the curve has gone too far while most of the risks we see remain relevant until October. Some of the key features: • Clearing: A central ledger records transactions, gold transfers and participant balances. Gold is settled on an unallocated basis, with deposits and withdrawals processed through designated vaults. Eligible settlement metal consists of internationally recognised 400oz (12.5kg) bars. Participation from global bullion banks, regulators and the SGE is intended to align the platform with international standards while maintaining strong links to China's financial system. • Vaulting: Hong Kong is positioning itself as a regional trading and reserve centre. Designated vaults are directly linked to the clearing system, while storage, refining and insurance capacity continue to expand. Plans call for more than 2,000 tonnes of vault capacity over time (for comparison, LBMA vaults stored 9,534tonnes of gold at the end of July). By linking pricing and trading to deliverable metal, Hong Kong seeks to combine physical logistics with financial infrastructure. • Pricing: HKPMCC has introduced the HAU benchmark, a Hong Kong-specific OTC gold reference price. Participating bullion banks submit bid and offer prices, which are aggregated into a benchmark published during Asian trading hours. records.text: Diverging margins and runs. Refined product supply and product margins n typically move together along the supply curve as demand shifts, but unprecedented supply constraints have driven a sharp divergence: global refinery runs are down 7mb/d year-over-year (yoy), while margins remain near record highs. We analyze the relationship between refinery runs and product margins and reiterate our constructive view on deferred margins. Capacity outages put a ceiling on runs. Three factors are constraining global n refinery runs despite record margins across regions and US utilization surging to 97%. First, Middle Eastern and Russian refineries are both operating at only 60% of capacity because of unplanned outages from drone and missile attacks. With nearly 10mb/d of global refining capacity currently offline, the 7mb/d yoy drop in runs is consistent with the strong historical negative relationship between outages and refinery runs. Second, China’s refined-product export quota restrictions are weighing on Chinese refinery runs. Third, still-elevated crude prices are curbing refiners’ buying appetite in countries with heavily regulated retail fuel prices. Margins and runs usually move together. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 20 August 2026 Citi Research 3 Our global forecast continues to be shaped by two competing factors. Second, despite the pressures and uncertainties associated with the conflict, our longstanding “resilience” theme remains in play. Global growth this year looks to be running at 2.6%, down a notch from last year but still solid given the magnitude of the shock. This markdown is reflected in both our DM and EM growth aggregates, with DM growth projected to be 1.5% versus 1.8% last year and EM growth at 4.0% versus 4.3% last year.1 As highlighted in Figure 2, these markdowns are spread broadly across a range of economies. Growth this year is seen to soften in Canada, the euro area, Japan, China, Brazil, and Chile. But some countries are successfully navigating the headwinds. records.text: Notably, refinery outages typically translate into a smaller than one-for-one decline in global refinery runs. We find that a 1mb/d increase in outages typically leads to a 0.6mb/d decrease in global refinery runs, as unaffected refineries start to run harder in response to higher margins. We also estimate that a 1mb/d increase in refinery outages leads to a $3/bbl increase in the fair value of US diesel margins after 12 months (or 14% historically in the sample from 2010). The boost to margins from outages is likely higher now because of limited effective spare capacity (especially in the US) and the larger-than-average effect from stock draws at low stock levels. Given the unclear prospects for near-term geopolitical de-escalation in the Middle East and especially in Russia, we do not see a swift decline in refinery outages and reiterate our view that margins are likely to remain well above historical averages for the foreseeable future, especially diesel. While expected 0.5mb/d capacity additions in India and the Middle East over the next 12 months should help to ease global refining constraints somewhat, they will be too small to offset current outages if attacks on Middle Eastern and Russian refineries persist. On the contrary, geopolitical de-escalation and any potential moderation in refinery outages should push refinery runs higher, allowing global supply to “cure” higher prices. Third, still-elevated crude prices are curbing refiners’ buying appetite in countries with heavily regulated retail fuel prices. Many governments have adopted a retail or a wholesale price ceilings to shield consumers from soaring energy costs (e.g., South Korea, Hungary, Thailand), preventing refiners from passing on high crude costs to final consumers and effectively reducing their margins. Margins and Runs Usually Move Together Outside of large supply shocks, the typical relationship between margins and runs is strongly positive. In the short run, elevated refinery runs tend to reflect refiners’ expectations of strong demand. Refinery margins would then increase to make operations profitable for a wider range of refineries, unlocking profits for higher-cost refineries that wouldn’t run under lower margins. This positive relationship between refinery runs and margins reflects a typical upward-sloping supply curve (Exhibit 5). An outage shock shifts the refineries’ supply curve to the left (or inward), reflecting a reduction in total capacity and implying that for each level of runs, margins need be higher. Higher margins also incentivize profitable refiners with extra spare operating capacity to increase supply. It also provides households with an alternative store of value at a time when confidence in property and domestic equities has been patchy. The strategy has been built over decades. China transformed gold from a tightly state- controlled venue into a more market-oriented system, with the launch of the Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE) in 2002 a critical step. The SGE allowed domestic trading to expand and created Chinese pricing, clearing and settlement capabilities. The objective was not only to increase ownership of bullion, but also to ensure that China did not remain entirely dependent on infrastructure and benchmarks centred in London and New York. Today China is simultaneously one of the world’s largest producers, importers and consumers of gold. That scale gives policymakers an incentive to capture more of the market infrastructure around trading, storage, refining and settlement. Domestic banks distribute physical gold and accumulation products, exchanges support renminbi- denominated trading, and official reserves have risen. The market has already become an ecosystem rather than a collection of isolated policy initiatives. Yet, China has more work to do and is pushing ahead. records.text: US Economic Perspectives19 August 2026 ab 22 Box: Rules of thumb for impacts of key economic shocks We usually rely on estimated time-series models to bring in the impact of various factors on our forecast. However, rules of thumb are often useful to give a rough idea of how important a shock is likely to be. Below are a few key rules of thumb that we use:  1 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate pushes down core inflation by 15bp.  Permanent $10 per barrel level shift in the price of Brent crude pushes up the level of CPI by 40bp and core CPI by 4bp.  A one percent decline in the dollar increases consumer import prices by 0.15 percent.  A one percent increase in import prices results in a 0.12 percent increase in core consumer prices.  A one percent increase in CRB spot food index equals about 8bp in prices of food at home with about 2/3rds in the first six months and 1/3rd in the six months after that. (CPI food at home is 8% of the CPI basket.)

These patterns confirm that, like in the US, AI-employment headwinds are visible in industries where labor-automating tools are already available. To more rigorously test the impact of AI on employment, we use data from Revelio Labs to regress occupation-level employment growth on our AI exposure scores for over 800 occupations in a cross-country panel. After controlling for country and industry fixed effects, we find that a 10% occupational exposure to AI is only associated with a 0.1pp drag to annual headcount growth in France, Canada, and the US (Exhibit 5). The effect is small or slightly positive elsewhere, suggesting that economy-wide hiring headwinds remain limited. London still accounts for roughly 70% of global gold trading volumes, but competition from Shanghai and Hong Kong is increasing. Market participants warn that failure to modernise could shift activity towards Asian hubs, particularly as initiatives such as HKPMCC combine clearing, physical delivery and local price benchmarks. Gold markets remain fragmented across bars, vaults, accounts and settlement systems (CME trades 100oz compared to London’s 400oz gold bars). Ownership transfers can be cumbersome (i.e. bars may have to be remelted/ recast), and smaller investors often face high minimum transaction sizes. Tokenisation could reduce these frictions while maintaining a direct link to physical metal. The EU has published its Electrification Action Plan, which set a target to boost the share of electricity in total energy demand by 1ppt annually until 2030 to 32%, compared to China’s target of 1ppt in the current five-year plan. While Europe’s energy demand is only 50% of China’s, this looks to support copper consumption. In China meanwhile, despite an air pocket in 2H25, copper demand has been resilient: operating rates at cable/wire manufacturers have recovered while inventories have declined, highlighting that electrification may come with ups and downs, but ultimately remains a structural driver. Hence, we continue to see upside to copper, especially once buyers return from the summer break. The result was EUR19.4bn of euro fonds outflows alongside a record EUR24.2bn of unit-linked inflows. Once that pressure eased, the rate differential reasserted itself, until the ECB hiking cycle pushed the Livret A to 3% in February 2023 against life insurance rates lagging near 1.9%, a gap widened further by the 17.2% social charges levied on euro fonds interest. Outflows peaked at EUR11.2bn in Q4 2022. The reversal has been equally abrupt: with credited rates repriced higher and the Livret A cut, Q1 2026 delivered EUR5.9bn of inflows, nearly matching the whole of 2025. Ramo I – slower cycle with structural scarring: Ramo I has followed a fundamentally different path to euro fonds, with net premium inflows remaining in positive territory from 2016 to 2022, through Covid and negative policy rates. Surrender penalties kept policyholders in place, and the ‘gestioni separate’ (the ringfenced bond portfolios backing Ramo I policies) delivered net returns that comfortably beat Italian bank deposits for most of the period. But those portfolios were slowly repricing lower, and by 2022 the net return to policy holders had compressed to roughly 1.4%. There is a significant chance that the growth target (4.5-5.0%) will be missed if no meaningful loosening measures are taken. We believe the government is committed to the target. There have been some signs of pick up in policy initiatives in recent days (see below for details). But we need a lot more both in terms of policy signals and actions. Deputy Minister of Finance Liao Min will host a press conference on fiscal policy tomorrow. This will be an informative meeting as fiscal policy needs to play a key role and Minister Liao is a technocrat who commands a lot of respect in the market. What the market wants to know is whether the focus is on implementation of existing policy plans or new measures. But it is clear this is not quite September 2024 yet when the press conferences were held by ministers instead of their deputies. Ultimately, we see value in selling CHF versus its main funding rival, the JPY on ongoing intervention risks, relative valuation and divergent central banks. The outlook for CHF vs USD is likely to be dominated by positioning: long USD/CHF has been the go-to carry trade in G10. But the recent decline is starting to weigh on front-end skew. Negative lending in July: New loan issuance contracted for the second time this year, falling by RMB340bn in July, echoing weak domestic demand. Household loans contracted by RMB460.3bn in July, corresponding to dire consumption as well as the unbated slump in home sales. On the corporate side, corporate bill financing – a category frequently used by banks to bolster credit figures during periods of weak credit demand – rose by RMB375.7bn. In contrast, short-term and medium- to long-term corporate loans declined by RMB250bn and RMB230bn, respectively, echoing negative FAI growth TSF not that bad: Despite feeble loan growth, total social financing rose by RMB1.4trn or 24.4% y/y in July, primarily driven by a 65.1% rise in corporate bond net issuance to RMB453.6bn, suggesting a shift toward direct financing by enterprises to benefit from funding costs being lower than for bank loans. New corporate equity financing rose by RMB62.3bn y/y to RMB112.8bn thanks to the boom in domestic IPO market for tech companies . The RMB69.4bn y/y increase in government bond net issuance to RMB1.32trn aligns with our expectations that faster fiscal spending will be a primary instrument to support growth in Q3. Philadelphia manufacturing survey improves further The FRB of Philadelphia's headline manufacturing index rose 6.0 points to 47.4 in August, its highest level since April 2021, after jumping 31.1 points to 41.4 in July. Adjusted to ISM weights, the index fell -0.6 points to 57.5, still a decent level. The Empire State headline index, the other regional survey out for August to date, also hung onto its July improvement (see our recap here). Overall, the suite of regional manufacturing surveys improved markedly in July. However, like the Empire State survey, details in the FRB of Philadelphia survey softened despite the further improvement in the headline business activity index.The new orders index fell -6.9 points to 30.1, while the shipments index fell -6.0 points to 27.7. Given the scale of the July improvement, however, both the new orders and shipments indexes remain at the upper end of the recent range. Prices indexes moderated. The prices paid index fell -13.0 points to 40.9 and the prices received index fell -9.7 points to 17.7. Both are now close to February levels, prior to the Middle East conflict. Data were collected from August 10 to August 17, a period that saw some slight firming in Brent crude oil prices, while retail gasoline prices moved sideways. Firms' expectations surged in August. The future general activity index rose 39.2 points to 73.6, the highest level since August 1983.

Furthermore, manufacturing employment saw a decline of about 127,200 jobs in 2025 – the weakest performance since 2008 – and investment fell to 22.2% of GDP in Q1 2026 from 24.4% in 2024 (Figure 3). This pattern suggests a transition towards export-oriented activity with limited domestic integration . The changing export mix brings deeper implications. The share of automotive exports (HS87) contracted from 27% in 2024 to 20.2% in May 2026, while that of computing and electronics components has risen (Figures 3 and 5). For example, automotive assembly traditionally offers high domestic content, dense supplier linkages, and significant intersectoral multipliers. In contrast, the expanding electronics segment involves shallower transformation of largely imported inputs, resulting in thinner domestic value addition. This compositional shift explains much of the export–output divergence, in our view. This electronics surge is driven by both tariff architecture and specific demand drivers. US investment in AI infrastructure has made data-center hardware Mexico’s fastest-growing export category; shipments of computers, servers and related equipment hit a record USD105.8bn between January and May (+84.5% y/y), overtaking automotive exports for the first time. Third, the attacks on Russia’s refineries keep refining margins under pressure, adding to the impact of higher crude prices. Fourth, LNG prices are under pressure as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and the refilling of storage tanks in Europe is running behind the schedule of previous years. Finally, EM currencies have generally weakened, with many sitting at their lows since the start of the war, thus increasing the likelihood of pass-through to domestic inflation. This comes at a time when the economy has proved more resilient than initially feared, with strong economic surprises and upward revisions to growth estimates. The key question for investors now is whether these earnings are good enough to support further price appreciation. Sadly, we doubt it, and here is why: • Beat weak expectations. The biggest earnings surprises came from Utilities, Health Care and Staples, three sectors carrying some of the lowest growth expectations (Figure 2) and accounting for just 25% of the market. Most of the actual earnings growth came from Energy, which more than doubled profits. Impressive, but only if oil prices keep behaving as though geopolitical risks are never going away. Meanwhile, Europe's heavyweight sectors, Financials and Industrials, delivered far more modest surprises. records.text: uanced. First, the lack of indirect price pressures in the aftermath of the spike in oil & gas prices does not mean these are unlikely to show up. As noted, wholesale costs relevant for the food retail sector have inflected higher. Food inflation is due to rise. It seems unlikely, however, that it will rise to anywhere near 7%Y peak, which was the Bank's initial estimate in the April MPR. Second-round effects, meanwhile, depend on the balance between slack in the economy and inflation perceptions of households and corporates (note, we would make a firm difference between perceptions, which we think are important, and expectations, which we see as a theoretical concept that is in any case just a beta to headline inflation). As things stand, with headline inflation in the 3%Y to 3.5%Y range, and the labour market as loose as it is, meaningful second-round effects – at a scale that would prolong the energy shock beyond mid-2027 – look implausible to us. As long as this assessment of the interplay between headline inflation and the slack in the economy is shared by the core of the MPC too, a hike is unlikely. Higher imports have narrowed the goods-trade balance this year and pushed the CA deep into deficit territory. Thailand’s high dependence on energy imports has added to these headwinds, further increasing THB’s sensitivity to oil-price moves and leaving it exposed to USD swings. The possibility of Fed hikes later this year would also widen rate differentials against THB, as the BoT is expected to keep monetary policy accommodative. De-escalation of Iran could be a near-term risk to bearish THB positions, as it would be associated with a weaker USD and lower oil. THB’s correlation with gold appears may also lead to more volatility. However, beyond these near-term risks to our bearish THB view, we see underlying THB flows staying weak this quarter before CA flows turn more favorable towards Dec. We forecast USDTHB at 33.7/USD by 3Q and 33/USD by end- 2026 but with rising risks of weaker CA flows weighing on THB for longer. records.text: 30 World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 Türkiye: TRY to outperform forwards Hande Kucuk MLI (UK) Mikhail Liluashvili MLI (UK) Themes: the carry trade is still on Our forecast remains below forwards as the central bank is committed to real currency appreciation and has sufficient reserves to meet the funding gap short term. The carry trade positioning has been steadily increasing recently almost reaching pre-war highs. Usable reserves coupled with gold reserves comfortably cover foreign FX positioning. Key macro developments: The CBRT has reversed most of its post-war FX sales, with cumulative net sales since end-February falling to around US$5bn from a peak of US$52bn in the first month of the conflict, based on our estimates. The recovery has been supported by seasonal tourism revenues, limited resident dollarisation and the return of short-term inflows. The CBRT's net FX position stood at US$50.9bn on 13 August, around US$20bn below pre-war levels, though roughly US$15bn of this gap reflects gold-price valuation effects rather than intervention. We therefore think reserve- related constraints on policy normalisation have largely eased, potentially allowing TLREF to decline from 40% towards the 37% policy rate after nearly six months of suspended one-week repo funding. We note that scrap supply and fabrication demand have proven less price- sensitive than expected, with holders reluctant to sell gold and end-users willing to absorb higher prices. Still, our model confirms that current investor buying is more consistent with a price closer to US$4,000/oz than US$5,000/oz, which is associated with investment demand growth of 21% YoY. Hence, investor purchases must accelerate for gold to push towards US$5,000/oz. Central bank purchases already provide a supportive backdrop, rising to 51t in June, well above the 12‑month average of 27t. However, a sustained move higher in gold would also require a recovery in ETF inflows. records.text: Running Hard or Hardly Running: Effect of Refinery Outages on Runs and Margins Diverging Margins and Runs Global refined product margins have risen over the last two months and are up $30 year-over year following the escalation in the Middle East, continuing attacks on Russian refineries, and gradually recovering global demand. Diesel margins — the epicenter of refined products’ tightness — rose to a new all-time high at above $100/bbl in the US, exceeding crude prices. However, refined product supply has been unable to respond to the rally in product margins, with global refinery runs still down nearly 7mb/d year-over-year (yoy) (Exhibit 1). This divergence is quite unusual because refined product supply and product margins typically move together along the supply curve as demand shifts. But unprecedented supply constraints on refining capacity from well-above normal refinery outages have curbed many refiners’ ability to increase production in response to higher prices (Exhibit 2). We analyze the relationship between refinery runs and product margins and the role of refinery outages in the joint dynamic of runs and prices, and reiterate our constructive view on deferred margins. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS Improving Sentiment Towards EM. Expectations for further Fed tightening have continued to recede following the FOMC pause and softer-than-expected CPI and PPI prints, providing an additional tailwind for EM assets. Our BRS factor flow data shows a notable improvement in both EM FX and equity flows over the past month compared to their DM counterparts (Figure 2) . The main exception remains EM bonds, where higher US Treasury yields have weighed on sovereign debt performance. However, as highlighted in this week's Theme (p1), the rise in long-end US yields has so far had only a limited impact on EM spreads and regional market volatility, especially with Fed’s recent commitment to support the long-end. While renewed geopolitical tensions could drive commodity prices higher and rekindle inflation concerns, EM central banks are generally entering this period from a position of strength, with greater policy credibility and stronger frameworks to anchor inflation expectations and manage capital flow volatility. Doubling Down on TWD. Our strategy remains unchanged as USD selling has intensified over the past two weeks: (1) long EM ex-Asia carry and beta, and (2) North Asia versus South Asia. records.text: 10 World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 CA rates: higher curve on strong data Katie Craig Ralph Axel BofAS BofAS Themes: CA rates higher as economy gains momentum Recent Canadian economic data have surprised stronger than anticipated, pushing CAD rates higher across the curve and repricing market expectations of near-term BoC hikes. While we acknowledge the risks around hikes are changing, we believe the market is continuing to overprice hikes. We continue to like being long duration and recommend clients fade market pricing of hikes. Our expectations for CA rates are dependent on our expectations for the BoC path. We continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold in '26, but stronger activity data increase the risk of hikes beginning in '27. The unemployment rate has consistently come in below expectations and has trended lower, suggesting the CA economy is gaining momentum. At the same time, wage growth slowed meaningfully in the July report, and CPI has eased, with median and trimmed measures currently around the BoC's 2% target. This mix argues that the BoC can remain patient, even as risks are shifting toward eventual future tightening. Despite tepid inflation, a technical recession earlier this year and a negative output gap, the market continues to price in more BoC hikes near-term. We keep a JPY long versus the CHF. EUR Real money demand for the EUR is positive once again and they are now net buyers. Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures The USMCA has transitioned to an annual review cycle following the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) decision not to confirm the 16-year extension requested by Mexico and Canada. Under Article 34.7.4, this activates mandatory annual joint reviews through 2036. However, we emphasize that the agreement has not lapsed: preferential tariffs, rules of origin, investment protections, and dispute settlement mechanisms remain fully in force. The 16-year extension is still an option, subject to written confirmation by the three heads of government at any given time. The third US–Mexico bilateral round (21–23 July) in Mexico City was described by both delegations as “constructive”. The agenda – covering steel/aluminum, automotive, economic security, labor, agriculture, and the substitution of Asian-origin inputs – aligns precisely with the structural pressure points identified in this report. Notably, the number of pending bilateral issues were narrowed from 54 to 14 prior to the round, with a fourth session scheduled for September in Washington DC. Mexico’s tariff exposure is currently defined by two active US instruments : ▪ Section 232: The 25% steel and aluminum regime (in effect since March 2025), which operates on sectoral grounds and remains unaffected by broader trade litigation . ▪ Section 122 & Section 301: The 10% Section 122 import surcharge expired on 24 July. In plain English, "underlying" hotels price inflation (CPI Accommodation Proxy is a category that attempts to mimic domestic holiday prices) is edging up, but in today's reading, the overall accommodation services inflation was dampened by the more volatile Overnight Stays sub-component. We think that due to staycations, hotels have a bit more pricing power this year. Catering inflation was soft. We don't think this was due to the government's VAT cut – the ONS wouldn't have sampled it. Indeed, it seems not much of the discounting, even in categories like Attractions or Soft Play, was picked up by the ONS. The flipside of this is that any upward pressure from these categories come September, when the VAT cut expires, ought to be modest. Finally, some of the more administrative price pressures ticked up – health insurance, for example – thus driving our estimate of underlying services inflation modestly higher (3.77%Y). Part of the recovery can be explained by the proximity of UK listed companies’ dividend season and the need for GBP. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Summary of the Solvency Capital Requirement: The Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) is the cornerstone of the European regulatory framework for insurers. It represents the amount of capital that an insurer must hold to ensure that, with 99.5 % probability, it can meet its obligations over the next 12 months. The Solvency II regulatory changes scheduled for January 2027 introduce meaningful changes to the way that the interest-rate SCR is calculated and have potential implications for how insurers might hedge interest rate risk to optimise their SCR. How SCR hedging interacts with liability discount curve hedging: For eurozone insurers with fixed cash flows, the focus extends beyond simply hedging the regulatory curve risk of their liabilities to also optimising their Solvency Ratio. As shown by the Solvency Ratio formula below, this means simultaneously managing the rate-risk exposure of both Own Funds and the SCR. The two components react differently, with Own Funds stability coming from closely hedging risk generated by the liability discount curve (discussed on the previous page), while the SCR is optimised by minimising the theoretical losses from the yield curve stress test shifts shown in Figure 9. records.text: US Economic Perspectives19 August 2026 ab 30 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Comparison to the forecast models As with most Phillips curve style models, our models were unable to forecast the inflation as it surged upward in 2021-2022 and, as expected, the majority of models were not a good guide as inflation has fallen. (Note that in the early part of 2022, the core PCE price inflation time-varying trend models and the component model remained above 4% throughout the forecast horizon, which at that point went through the end of 2024, compared to the 2.8% that has been published for 2024 inflation.) In particular, the models do not include an effect for changes in the mix of demand and the supply constraints that hampered efforts to satisfy this changing mix. We believe the combined effects of the changing demand mix and supply issues were far more important in driving the initial inflation surge in 2021 than were the standard Phillips curve driver of aggregate resource slack, though fiscal spending and monetary policy have likely accounted for a fair amount of the reason that inflation did not fall faster from that peak. The models now project core PCE inflation of 3.5% to 4.0% this year (compared to our 3.2% pre-revision baseline) and 2.7% to 3.7% next year (compared to our 2.4% baseline). records.text: China Economic Comment20 August 2026 ab 2 broader HPF withdrawal requirements, and measures supporting housing inventory destocking. Nationally, China released the amendments to the rules managing housing provident fund on August 18th. The latest rules expand the permitted use of HPF funds, streamline the withdrawal process, while assign State Council authority to set HPF rate adjustments. Fiscal policy: The NDRC called for faster implementation of the RMB800bn policy financing tool announced at the March NPC, compared with RMB500bn in 2025. Reportedly, the 2026 implementation guidelines have been circulated to local governments with fiscal interest subsidies for eligible projects. Consumption: Nine ministries together issued new guidelines aimed at boosting consumption in county-level markets. The measures focus on upgrading commercial infrastructure, improving services, expanding supplies, and enhancing logistics networks. That said, the guideline did not announce a quantified fiscal package. Monetary policy: The PBOC released its Q2 Monetary Policy Report, reiterating its accommodative policy stance. However, the report contained no new easing measures and removed the previous reference to lowering banks’ funding costs, suggesting a reduced likelihood of an RRR cut in the near term. Consistent with this signal, the August LPR fixing was left unchanged.

records.text: US Economic Perspectives19 August 2026 ab 34 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Incoming data and forecast for hourly wages Wage and employee compensation growth continues to slow. Average hourly earnings increased only 0.05% in July with both the 12-month and 3-month change the lowest since a temporary pandemic-induced plunge in 2021. 12-month AHE growth has now returned to the pace in the 24 months prior to the pandemic. Other measures of wage growth, on balance, have shown less slowing (though they are more lagged than AHE) and are consistent with a continued gradual downtrend in wage and labor compensation growth. In particular the 12-month change in the Employment Cost Index (ECI) for total compensation of private sector workers stepped down to 3.3% in June from 3.4% in March, and its lowest pace since 2021, but still ¼ to ½ pp above its pace in the couple of years prior to the pandemic. We expect a bit more slowing in wage growth over the next 3 to 6 months, though the lagged impact of higher price inflation, and expectations of higher productivity, should lead to a moderate uptick further out in the forecast. And the primary impact is not a cessation of activity, but rather a structural shift in production composition and a reduction in the domestic value-added (DVA)captured by Mexico. Increasingly, Mexico’s export boom is decoupling from its industrial production, a phenomenon driven by a shift towards lower-value-added assembly. Whether Mexico can reverse this trend and raise DVA is core to the ‘corridor thesis’: namely, the risk that Mexico serves as a high-volume pass-through for foreign content rather than developing a deep production base . records.text: 4 World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 USD: losing steam Alex Cohen BofAS Themes: the rising bar for Fed hikes Wind has been taken out of the USD’s sails over the past month, driven by developments on the economic data and Fed expectations fronts. The DXY traded at fresh 12-month highs in June and most of July amid upside employment and inflation readings, and initially hawkish comments from incoming fed chair Wash (expressing concern over persistently above target inflation). However, after Warsh’s comments at the July FOMC stopped short of articulating a policy prescription for reducing inflation, the DXY fell back into its well established range. Subsequently, July CPI reflected signs of moderating inflationary pressure, while the July employment report similarly failed to show a resurgence and hiring or wages. Collectively, this is reduced market expectations for Fed hikes this year, which now sit at slightly less than one hike by December, down from around two hikes just prior to the July FOMC. The outlook for the USD appears more neutral for the remainder of the year. Forecasts: Unchanged outside of CAD and JPY We leave most of our USD bilateral forecasts unchanged, consistent with a modestly overvalued USD. We continue to see EUR/USD ending the year at 1.15. Separately, we now see further downside in USD/JPY, but this is more about changing dynamics in Japan and the rising risks of further coordinated intervention activity. We also revised our USD-CAD forecasts as well.

LLC Global Economics Comment: Is AI Impacting Global Labor Markets? 19 August 2026 | 12:29AM EDT Our prior work has found visible but narrow AI-related labor market impacts in n the US, but evidence in other economies is more limited. In this Global Economics Comment, we assess the extent to which AI is creating labor market headwinds outside of the US. After extracting a common signal from eleven adoption surveys, we find that n adoption rates are quite similar across DMs. France and the US lead with adoption rates around 20%, while adoption rates in other DMs fall in the 15-20% range and EM adoption rates are slightly lagging at 10-15%. Using official cross-country labor market data, we find similar (albeit generally n more muted) labor market impacts as those documented in the US. We find a negative correlation between AI exposure scores and change in job openings since 2022H2. We also observe employment underperformance in non-US DMs in the information services industry and other high-exposure subsectors such as call centers, management consulting, and advertising. To size the overall hiring headwind at a country level, we regress occupation-level n employment growth on our detailed occupation AI exposure scores in a cross-country panel. A 10% AI exposure score is associated with only a 0.1pp drag to annual occupational headcount

On an aggregate basis, the duty actually paid on total US imports from Mexico rises to just 3.7% in 2026 [0.2% in 2024]; despite higher statutory walls, the surge in USMCA compliance effectively anchors the rate. However, the underlying divergence is stark. While the auto parts and components network (wiring harnesses, boards, transformers) maintains high compliance, passenger and goods vehicles now bear a calculated duty of 11–14%. This suggests Section 232 is acting as a tax on final assembly rather than on the upstream supplier chain. Furthermore, concentration compounds this fragility. Data-processing machines alone account for 22.1% of the export flow in 2026. This leaves more than one-fifth of Me xico’s exports to the US dependent on a single tariff line, the qualification of which rests on the very rules the USMCA review is designed to scrutinize. A second front is emerging in the white goods sector: Despite USMCA compliance rates exceeding 70%, air-conditioning machines (8415) and refrigerators (8418) show calculated duties rising to 4.7% and 12% respectively this year. The strength in portfolio management and investment advice services is largely tied to the strong stock market growth over the past year rather than the typical consumer demand and supply drivers that we usually think of as causing inflation. The largest contributor to core PCE price inflation being above its pre-pandemic pace is information processing equipment, which is likely a response to the boom in demand from AI investment for computing power. To overcome this limitation, we compile 11 surveys that measure AI adoption across countries and extract an ordinal ranking using the Bradley-Terry model (an algorithm which statistically constructs an overall ranking based on the observed pairwise rankings in unbalanced surveys where adoption is measured inconsistently). After rescaling around the OECD’s adoption survey —the most globally comprehensive measure in our compiled data—we unsurprisingly find that major DMs are ahead of other countries in deploying AI with adoption rates between 15-20% (Exhibit 1). Among DMs, France, the US, the Netherlands, and the UK score at the top end of this range, while Italy, Japan, and New Zealand score at the bottom end. Among major EMs, we estimate adoption rates between 10-15%. To identify whether AI is presently causing a pullback in labor demand, we regress Indeed.com industry job openings for major DMs on our industry-level AI exposure scores. We find that industries with greater exposure to AI automation are associated with slower job openings growth since the second half of 2022, with a more negative relationship in Germany, Australia, and the US (Exhibit 2). This is primarily backed by strong growth outturn that led to tightening by MAS in the last policy meeting. SNEER movements have correlated more with oil-price fluctuations, USD, and shifts in risk sentiment (inversely with all three factors). This is because still-low SGD rates have kept carry on short SNEER positions elevated. In addition, the possibility of Fed hikes later this year and USD strength could trigger a SNEER correction within the band. MAS’ ‘very slight’ tightening at the July meeting reduces negative carry on SNEER by 25bps annualized by our estimate. A faster pace of policy-led SNEER band appreciation would make it less prohibitive for markets to maintain long SNEER positions. However, negative carry still remains attractive at around 60bps annualized compared to low volatility in SNEER. On a bilateral basis, USD moves remain the key driver of USD/SGD, driven more by Fed- hike pricing, which may support USD through wider rate differentials versus peers. The break came in Q1 2023, when the ECB deposit rate of 3% left Ramo I visibly uncompetitive and quarterly flows swung to −EUR4.2bn, the first negative quarter since 2016. Ramo I net premium flows have recovered gradually but consistently since Q3 2024, reaching EUR2.4bn by Q4 2025. Two things are driving it: as ECB policy rates have fallen, the yield advantage bank deposits held over Ramo I has largely gone, restoring the product’s appeal to new buyers. At the same time the surrender wave has run its course, with the annual surrender rate easing from 10.3% in 2024 to 9.4% in 2025, as some of those policyholder who intended to exit have already done so. Cyclical or structural: Net premium inflows have resumed in both markets, although the drivers and pace of recovery differ. The rebound in French euro fonds inflows is cyclical and given the absence of exit costs, readily reversible should the spread against the Livret A turn again. In Italy, falling ECB policy rates provide a supportive backdrop for Ramo I, though part of the recovery also reflects the exhaustion of an earlier surrender wave. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is exploring how tokenised gold could be regulated, including digital tokens representing ownership of vaulted bullion. This is challenging because the FCA does not regulate spot physical gold markets, although it oversees derivatives and listed investment products. Digitalisation has a strategic dimension. London, Hong Kong and Shanghai are competing not only for trading volumes but also to establish the standards governing how gold is cleared, stored, traced and transferred. London benefits from its deep OTC market, extensive vault network and established standards. Hong Kong and Shanghai, however, offer proximity to the world's largest physical gold market and the opportunity to build modern infrastructure without legacy constraints. Tokenisation may reduce the importance of geography, but it increases the importance of standards, interoperability and network effects. Five structural trends support this transition: advances in blockchain technology, wealth transfer to younger investors, growing demand for traceable assets, expansion of tokenised real-world assets and continued geopolitical uncertainty. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Product overview: In the French life insurance market, euro fonds are the primary savings vehicle. Policyholders contribute to a pooled bond portfolio managed by the insurer, receiving a guaranteed minimum return plus a performance-based credited rate. Because capital is guaranteed and the product offers near daily liquidity with no surrender penalty, it functions more like a deposit account than a traditional contract. Italy’s Ramo I is the structural equivalent, but its exit terms are critically different, with surrender penalties typically running between 2% and 5% of accumulated value within the first five years. That single difference, the cost of leaving, helps explain why net premium inflows in the two markets respond differently to the same interest rate environment. Euro fonds – liquid product driven by rate arbitrage and regulatory capital: Flows into the French euro fonds are heavily influenced by the spread against the livret A, the tax-free state-guaranteed savings account whose quoted rate is the exact net return the saver receives. The 2017 outflows represent the one instance that doesn’t fit the pattern. Euro fonds were comfortably out-yielding the Livret A, but Solvency II had made them far more capital-intensive than unit-linked alternatives, insurers actively discouraged inflows by setting minimum unit-linked allocation requirements and raising entry fees. Core PCE is not.  Core CPI inflation edged down further in July — essentially returning to its post- pandemic low from February and only around 0.2pp above the level consistent with the FOMC's 2.0% PCE inflation target. records.text: and the role of gold China has long sought to internationalise the renminbi, but capital controls and limited convertibility have constrained progress. Internationalising a currency requires more than trade settlement; foreign investors also need clearing infrastructure, liquid assets and confidence that capital can move freely. Gold helps bridge some of these constraints because it is globally accepted, politically neutral and independent of any sovereign issuer. To internationalise CNY, China's strategy has focused on four areas. First, it has promoted the use of RMB in trade settlement. Second, it has developed offshore RMB centres, particularly Hong Kong, with RMB deposits, clearing banks, Bond Connect and Stock Connect programmes. Third, it has built RMB-denominated commodity markets, including gold, oil and iron ore, which means that a greater share of trade can now be priced and settled in CNY. Finally, China has invested heavily in payment infrastructure, including RMB clearing banks, the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System and bilateral central-bank swap lines. Gold is particularly useful because RMB-denominated gold links commodity demand with currency use. Foreign central banks, sovereign investors and trading firms may be more willing to hold an RMB claim backed by physical gold than an unsecured RMB cash balance, allowing China to gradually expand the currency's international use without fully liberalising the capital account. CNY internationalisation and HKPMCC support gold prices Beyond that, it is worth noting that China’s gold imports have posted a series of all-time highs YTD. Why? Also because China views gold as a strategic tool to support the internationalisation of CNY. By linking gold markets more closely to RMB-denominated trading, clearing and settlement, Beijing is gradually expanding alternatives to the dollar- centric financial system. HKPMCC represents an important step in that strategy. Combining clearing, vaulting, physical delivery and benchmark pricing should help position Hong Kong as the offshore hub linking with mainland China's gold market. Simultaneously, gold is becoming a digital asset too As competition for market share is increasing, gold is beginning to digitalise. Indeed, London, Hong Kong and Shanghai are increasingly competing not only for trading volumes but also for the standards governing how gold is stored, settled and transferred. If regulatory and technical hurdles can be overcome, digital gold could broaden ownership and create new sources of demand. The July CPI was a relatively encouraging report for inflation gradually progressing to target: The headline CPI increased only 0.07%, and 12-month headline CPI inflation, while it is still elevated at 3.36% (largely from a 25% increase in gasoline prices over the past year), fell 0.17pp in July and is down considerably from its 4.25% peak just two months ago. In contrast, the interest rate shock scenario used to calculate the SCR affects the entire yield curve (to varying amounts), meaning that even if liability interest rate risk is perfectly hedged versus the regulatory discount curve, a meaningful SCR can still lower the Solvency Ratio. Finding the correct balance of hedges can be difficult for insurers, as hedging the additional SCR interest rate risk with linear instruments would increase the volatility of Own Funds (by mismatching hedges vs the liability discount curve) and therefore the Solvency Ratio. Most insurers split the job by using linear instruments (e.g. bonds, swaps) to hedge the baseline Own Funds exposure and adding an option layer to cover the residual SCR asymmetries, preserving the effectiveness of linear hedges. records.text: World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 37 Mexico Carlos Capistran BofAS Banxico stays on hold at 6.50% in July Banxico kept the policy rate unchanged at 6.50% at its August meeting in a unanimous vote (see report), leaving its forward guidance intact and continuing to signal a prolonged pause. The Board pointed to the inflation outlook, the level of the peso, weak demand, and the current degree of monetary restriction as the drivers of the decision, and it still flags slack in the economy even after the strong 2Q GDP rebound. Notably, Banxico pushed back its convergence to the 3% target by two quarters, to 4Q 2027, though we continue to see inflation running above its path, in part due to persistent core. We read little into the delay: it rules out cuts in the coming months but does not, in our view, point to hikes. We continue to expect Banxico on hold at 6.50% all the way to the mid-2027 elections, and to stay there even if the Fed hikes in the following months. Risks to our call are balanced: to the downside, weak activity and a strong peso; to the upside, more persistent inflation or tighter Fed policy. records.text: Capacity Outages Put a Ceiling on Runs Three main factors are weighing on global refinery runs despite record margins across regions. First, large unplanned refinery outages in the Middle East and Russia from drone and missile attacks put more pressure on an already constrained global refinery system (Exhibit 3). Following recent attacks on the 0.4mb/d Jazan refinery in Saudi Arabia and ongoing repairs at refineries hit in March and April, Middle East outages remain 2mb/d above seasonal norms. Continuing drone attacks on Russian refineries keep Russian outages 3mb/d above seasonal norms. As a result, Middle Eastern and Russian refineries are both operating at only 60% of their respective capacities, down 18-20pp in August so far yoy (Exhibit 4). At the same time, US refineries, which have been unconstrained by large outages, have increased their average utilization rates by 3pp year-to-date in response to strong product margins. However, with the US utilization rate already in the high 90s, further supply increases could be challenging, while postponed maintenance typically increases the risks of later unplanned outages. A simulated 10% decline in automotive shipments resulted in a 0.3% reduction in economy-wide gross value added (GVA) and a loss of about 164,000 jobs. We view these results as illustrative multipliers that reflect the current productive structure rather than formal forecasts . Substantive insight from sectoral incidence, propagation: Manufacturing would account for MXN24bn of the GVA reduction (52% of the total), while the remaining 48% would accrue to non-manufacturing sectors including agriculture, mining, electricity, and wholesale trade, which would see GVA declines of between 0.4–0.6% (Figure 10). The implied multiplier is roughly 1.9, so for every peso of GVA lost directly in manufacturing, a further 0.9 pesos is lost in the broader economy. This framework treats many of its components as contrarian indicators – for example, historically low volatility and loose financial conditions is a warning signal that conditions could tighten (Figure 2). There remain indicators that still appear to favour remaining pro- risk at present : ▪ Positioning rebuilding but still not crowded: The risk recovery continues to correspond with a gradual rebuilding of positioning in equities. With scores of 63 for the US, 37 for Europe and 65 for Japan, positioning still does not appear a headwind to further equity gains (Figures 3 and 4). ▪ Valuations show risk assets no longer cheap, but not yet overbought: MarFA™ mispricings for risk assets are slowly turning to indicate more overbought assets than oversold assets (Figures 3 and 4). For example, there is now only one major regional index that appears significantly oversold – MSCI Mexico. However, there remain very few risk-assets that appear significantly overbought. Yet those flows are drawing down already tight US inventories, the only major hub open for business, creating a global competition for fuel that is pushing up diesel cracks. Demand destruction is coming, but likely at higher prices Harvest-related demand growth, low inventories, and ongoing supply outages may outweigh early signs of demand destruction. Our outlook for diesel remains bullish through the balance of 2026 (or until Hormuz flows normalize). In short, absent a meaningful supply recovery, the diesel market appears poised to stay tight, volatile, and expensive well into next year. We expect ICE gasoil cracks to average roughly $67/bbl in 3Q26 and $62/bbl in 4Q26. Unless Middle East, China and/or Russia supply issues are resolved, diesel prices are likely to remain near cycle highs, with further upside risk if inventories continue to draw into the winter. First, the conflict in Iran remains unresolved and the Strait of Hormuz is still largely closed. Oil prices have generally traded at or below $90/barrel in recent weeks, reflecting signals that President Trump continues to seek an exit from the conflict, but the associated uncertainties remain elevated. Second, despite headwinds from the conflict, the global economy continues to expand at a solid pace, which highlights our longstanding “resilience” theme. Global growth this year is running at a 2.6% pace, down a notch from last year but still solid given the magnitude of the shocks. All told, we see appreciable (two-sided) risks to our forecasts for both growth and inflation. These include the trajectory of oil prices, as well as simmering pressures in bond markets reflecting fiscal challenges in many countries. Our resilience theme is reinforced by recent economic indicators—The global services PMI has rebounded after retreating at the onset of the Iran conflict and remains comfortably above 50. A 10% AI exposure score is associated with only a 0.1pp drag to annual occupational headcount growth in France, Canada, and the US, with negligible effects elsewhere. Negative effects are more visible after restricting to entry-level employees or occupations with high displacement risk, but global AI-related hiring headwinds still appear confined to a narrow set of industries and workers. Is AI Impacting Global Labor Markets? The impacts of artificial intelligence on labor markets are a major question for the labor market and economic outlook. While much of the focus has been on the US— where richer labor market data point to visible labor market effects that are still narrowly confined to a limited set of industries—there are also questions about how AI is affecting labor markets in other economies. In this Global Economics Comment, we consider a harmonized set of indicators to assess the extent to which AI is creating global labor market headwinds. The timing and extent of AI-driven labor headwinds naturally depends on the rate of AI adoption among firms. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Summary of the Solvency II extrapolation: Under the Solvency II framework, insurers build their risk-free rate (RFR) curve based on 6m Euribor swaps out to 20 years (known as the Last Liquid Point), and beyond this point the RFR curve gradually converges towards the Ultimate Forward Rate (UFR), currently set at 3.3%, using the Smith-Wilson (SW) extrapolation method. Full convergence to the UFR occurs by year 60. The resultant RFR curve is then supplemented by the VA to generate the discount curve for an insurer’s best estimated liabilities. For an in-depth analysis of the Solvency II yield curve extrapolation and upcoming changes, please see Impact of new Solvency II extrapolation, dated 3 February. Key changes ▪ New long-dated risk: Rather than using the 20y swap as the starting point for the extrapolation, the new method, called the Alternative Method (AM), instead uses the Last Liquid Forward Rate (LLFR), which combines forward swap rates from 15y to 50y, weighted by the traded swap volume at the different pillar points on the curve (i.e. 20y, 25y, 30y, 40y and 50y). ▪ Optional five-year scale-in for extrapolation changes: Insurers are allowed to choose between adopting the full extrapolation change on 30 January 2027 or scaling in the changes over a five-year period from 2027 to 2032. records.text: 8 World at a Glance | 19 August 2026 JPY: patiently bullish Shusuke Yamada BofAS Japan Themes: four stakeholders in FX intervention The current yen-buying intervention framework involves four key players: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MoF), the US Treasury, the Takaichi administration, and the Bank of Japan (BoJ). Yet their degree of alignment is unclear given differences in mandates and policy objectives. Their views may differ on several questions: Is the exchange rate itself the policy target? Which policy tools should be used to influence FX markets? Is the current level of the yen problematic? How well do they understand financial markets? Although four parties are involved, their objectives are unlikely to be identical. Policy options to support the yen include FX intervention by the Japanese and US authorities, BoJ rate hikes, and fiscal or broader economic measures by the government. Intervention can also affect the incentives and effectiveness of other policy tools. There is also growing speculation that Prime Minister Takaichi could reshuffle the cabinet by September. It is unclear whether and how intervention developments would influence personnel decisions, but political considerations cannot be ruled out. For details, see report: Japan Rates and FX Watch: Yen-buying intervention: Reading the authorities’ intent after US CPI 12 August 2026. Chairman Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole strikes us as a good venue to address these issues. He has the opportunity to explain how he sees the economy and the transmission of monetary policy. This could also entail a description of his strategy to bring inflation down and some insight regarding his reaction function. If he fails to tackle these issues head on, he ultimately may be pressed to demonstrate his inflation-fighting commitment by actually hiking rates. Our reading of the macro fundamentals leaves us doubtful that rate hikes are necessary but, at some point, central bankers must act as necessary to defend their credibility. In Europe, the challenges facing monetary policy strike us as somewhat less acute than in the United States and Japan. That said, the life of a central banker is never easy. Consistent with this, we see the Bank of England remaining on hold this year and cutting next year, defying market expectations of tightening . records.text: Using our model, we find that historically, a $10/bbl rise in the US average of gasoline and diesel margins tends to boost global refinery runs by 0.6-0.8mb/d the following month (Exhibit 8).1 At the same time, we estimate that a persistent 1mb/d decrease in global refinery runs lowers US diesel margins by $0.7/bbl via a lower utilization rate within a month, but boosts margins by $6/bbl after 12 months or by 27% in a sample from 2010 (Exhibit 9). Central bank buying also provides downside support. With our US economists expecting the Fed to remain on hold, we see scope for gold to exceed $5,000/oz in 2027, potentially earlier. That said, incoming US data, especially inflation, could drive volatility, while COMEX shorts near their lowest since April 2020 leave less scope for further short covering. Further growth deceleration: July’s economic data came in weaker than market and our expectations. Output growth slowed to 4.5% y/y for industrial production and 4.3% for services from Q2 averages of 4.6% and 4.5%, respectively. That implies GDP growth of 4.1% y/y in July, about 0.2pp less than both the Q2 average and the H2 rate needed to reach the full-year target of 4.5–5%. The National Bureau of Statistics noted short-term disruptions from high temperatures, heavy rainfall and floods to industrial production in the month . Focusing on implementation, not new stimulus: When the Politburo held its quarterly economic work meeting on 30 July, it had likely already received the economic data for July.
